text: When the porters wife announced that a gentleman and a lady wished to see me, I had, the wish being father to the thought, an immediate vision of sitters who had come for portraits. <break time="0.8s" /> The visitors, a tall, straight gentleman of about fifty and a slim, handsome lady, were dressed with such care and quiet distinction that I took it for granted they had come to be painted. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet when the lady said that they had come from Mister Rivet, a landscape painter I knew, the gentleman hesitated for a long moment before he could bring himself to state their errand. <break time="0.8s" /> I was then an illustrator for magazines and popular novels, but I could not get out of my head the honours, to say nothing of the rewards, of a great painter of portraits. <break time="0.8s" /> Illustration was my pot boiler, the work that paid the rent, and so it was with a sinking heart that I began to suspect these splendid strangers were not customers at all. <break time="0.8s" /> At last the Major, for such he proved to be, explained with painful frankness that they had lost their money and that they hoped to earn something as models for an artist like me. <break time="0.8s" /> We thought that if you ever have to do people like us, we might be something like it, said the Major, adding that his wife would be particularly good as a lady in a book. <break time="0.8s" /> Looking at them, so tall and so correct, I saw at once what they meant, for they were exactly the kind of people that my illustrations were always trying, and often failing, to suggest.
